n: The inner east gate stays closed on the six working days but opens on the Sabbath and the new moon. Holy time and holy space work together: special days bring special access.

f.w: on the sabbath it shall be opened

n: The prince stands at the gate’s threshold while priests offer his sacrifices. He worships but does not go into the priests’ inner court—even a ruler has limits before God.

f.w: he shall worship at the threshold of the gate
f.g: The prince bows in worship at the doorway rather than entering the priests’ court.

n: The common people also worship at the entrance to this gate on Sabbaths and new moons, sharing in the view toward God’s house.
The prince’s Sabbath offering is six lambs and a ram—larger than the Sabbath offering in the Law of Moses.
Grain offerings accompany the animals: an ephah for the ram and whatever the prince can afford for the lambs, with oil.

f.w: as he shall be able to give
f.g: Literally “the gift of his hand”—as much as he wishes.

n: On the new moon, a young bull is added to the lambs and ram—marking the start of each month with worship.
The grain offering is matched to each animal, with flexibility for the lambs according to what he can give.

f.w: according as his hand shall attain unto
f.g: As much as he is able.

n: The prince enters and leaves through the same gate vestibule.
At the great festivals, worshippers who come in by the north gate leave by the south, and vice versa. This keeps crowds flowing—and symbolically, no one leaves God’s presence the same way they came.

f.w: he shall not return by the way of the gate whereby he came in
f.g: Many readers see a lesson here: worship should change the worshipper’s direction.

n: On festival days the prince worships among the people, going in and out with them—a leader who stands with his people, not above them.
Grain offerings at feasts follow the same measures given for the Sabbath and new moon.
For freewill offerings—gifts given beyond what is required—the east gate is opened for the prince and then shut after he leaves.

f.g: A freewill offering, given from gratitude, not obligation.

n: Every morning a year-old lamb is offered as a burnt offering—daily devotion at the start of each day.
Fine flour and oil accompany the morning lamb as a perpetual ordinance.
This continual offering is a constant reminder of Israel’s covenant with God, renewed each day.
If the prince gives land to one of his sons, it becomes the son’s permanent inheritance.
If he gives land to a servant, it returns to the prince in the year of liberty. Royal land stays in the family and cannot be used to build a power network.

f.g: The Jubilee year, every fiftieth year, when land returned to its original owners.

n: The prince may not seize the people’s land to enrich his family. This guards ordinary Israelites from royal greed and keeps families on their inherited land.

f.w: the prince shall not take of the people's inheritance

n: Ezekiel is led to the priests’ chambers on the north side and shown a place at the far west end.
Here priests cook the guilt and sin offerings and bake the grain offerings, so holy food is not carried into the outer court where people might contact it.

f.g: Contact with most holy things would bring people under special ritual restrictions.

n: Back in the outer court, Ezekiel sees a small court in each of its four corners.
The four corner courts are equal in size, forty by thirty cubits.

f.g: Possibly “enclosed” or “small” courts; the Hebrew is uncertain.

n: Each corner court has a low wall with hearths built beneath it for cooking.
These are kitchens where the Levites cook the people’s sacrifices for sacred meals. Worship included joyful communal meals in God’s presence.

f.g: Peace offerings eaten by worshippers and their families.
